x: The question contrasts Earth's fluid (outer) core with the Moon's core, which books describe as solid; the Moon has in fact a small solid inner core with a fluid outer layer (NASA 2011). Off-topic (solar system), moved.
source: https://www.astronomy.com/science/nasa-research-team-reveals-the-moon-has-earthlike-core/ (NASA 2011: solid iron-rich inner core ~240 km, fluid outer core ~330 km); app notes 4:5 sub 2
dispute: Key / books: solid. Strictly the Moon, like Earth, has a solid inner core inside a fluid outer core (NASA 2011, Weber et al.).

x: Shale → slate, limestone → marble, coal → diamond (the textbook pairing; strictly graphite), sandstone → quartzite. Moved to rocks.
source: NCERT Class 7 Geography ch.2 (rocks); NCERT Class 11 ch.5
evidence: only option 2 has A-iii, B-iv, D-i, the three certain pairs
dispute: Key / textbooks: coal → diamond. Strictly coal metamorphoses to anthracite/graphite; diamonds form from carbon in the mantle, not from coal.

x: The weather-map symbols used in the Indian Daily Weather Report were approved by the International Meteorological Organisation (in 1935, at Warsaw); the IMO became the WMO in 1950, which now standardises them. The '1998' in the stem is wrong, but IMO is the only meteorological body offered.
source: slideshare.net/slideshow/dgngng/265504538 (Interpretation of Indian Daily Weather Report: 'plan of symbols ... approved by the International Meteorological Organisation, Warsaw, 1935'); NCERT Practical Geography (kegy308) – symbols standardised by WMO
evidence: NCERT Class 11 Practical Geography ch.8 (WMO standardisation)

x: 'Congra' is read as the Kangra valley of the Himalayas, which is in Himachal Pradesh.
source: NextGen Indian Geography APPSC 04 (src/geography/nextgen-indian-geography-appsc-04.txt) p.10 (Himachal Himalaya valleys: Kashmir, Kangra, Kulu, Lahul-Spiti)

x: Karewas (Vudr) are lacustrine deposits of unconsolidated gravel and mud with glacial clay, forming terraces in the Kashmir Valley; they are famous for saffron (zafran). They were laid down when the Pleistocene lake of Kashmir drained (Plio-Pleistocene), so 'Tertiary' is loose. The other options describe Ganga khadar, coral reefs and volcanoes.
source: NextGen Indian Geography APPSC 02 (src/geography/nextgen-indian-geography-appsc-02.txt) p.12 (lacustrine gravel and mud; 'Karewas' or 'Vudr'); PMF Indian Physical Geography 01 p.53-54 (Pleistocene lake; saffron)
dispute: Option wording: Tertiary. Strictly the Karewas are Plio-Pleistocene lacustrine deposits, mostly Pleistocene (PMF Physical Geography 01 p.53).

x: Malwa is the region of Punjab south of the Sutlej (beyond the Beas–Sutlej doab); Majha lies between the Ravi and Beas, Doaba between the Beas and Sutlej.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 01 (src/geography/pmf-indian-physical-geography-01.txt) p.77 ('To the south of the Sutlej River lies the Malwa Plain of Punjab'); NextGen Indian Geography 04 p.14 (Malwa plain between Sutlej and Yamuna)
dispute: Official key: Malwa. Strictly: Malwa lies south of the Sutlej (PMF p.77); the land just south/east of the Beas is Doaba (Bist Doab).

x: The Cuddapah system was formed by deposition of unfossiliferous clay, slates, sandstones and limestones in synclinal basins; gneiss belongs to the older Archaean basement. Off-topic (rock systems), moved.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 01 (src/geography/pmf-indian-physical-geography-01.txt) p.26 ('deposition of unfossiliferous clay, slates, sandstones and limestones'); NextGen AP Geography 02 p.6

x: The APPSC key places the Sirasanambedu, Kovanur and Suramala iron-ore mines in Chittoor district (the old Chittoor–Nellore border belt of the south).
source: APPSC JL 2020 key; IBM mining plan https://ibm.gov.in/writereaddata/files/04222021131720SIRASANAMBEDU MINE.pdf (Sirasanambedu village, Pellakur mandal, SPSR Nellore district)
dispute: APPSC key: Chittoor. Strictly IBM records the Sirasanambedu iron-ore mine in Pellakur mandal, SPSR Nellore district (now Tirupati district), not an option.

x: The key marks only II incorrect: asbestos resists heat (I true), but India now has no asbestos production and Rajasthan holds most resources.
dispute: Key: Only II. Strictly Andhra Pradesh (Kadapa chrysotile) was India's only asbestos-producing State until 2013-14, so II was true then; no production since 2014-15 (IMYB 2022 Asbestos; Lok Sabha reply cited in web search).

x: The key is apatite: AP (Kasipatnam, Visakhapatnam) ranks first in apatite and was its producer; calcite, bauxite and dolomite come from several States.
source: Rocket AP Geography (src/geography/rocket-ap-geography.txt) p.2 ('1st place in Vermiculite & Apatite'), p.18 (Kasipatnam – 1st in reserves & production)
evidence: IMYB Apatite & Rock Phosphate 2017-18 (web search result)
dispute: Key: apatite. Strictly IMYB reports India's apatite production as nil since 2016-17, and AP's true sole-producer mineral is barytes (IMYB Apatite & Rock Phosphate reviews, web search).
